text.tspan: Installation
Gilbert has a width of 10hp and a depth of 38.1mm (1.5 inches). Gilbert draws 25ma from
both the +12V and -12V power rails and is reverse power protected.
Before placing Gilbert in your rack, turn off the power to your Eurorack case and then
properly install the power ribbon cable on both the module and your case's PSU bus
board.
Gilbert comes with a keyed power header, the key on the ribbon cable must align with
the notch on the power header. The red line on the ribbon cable must align with the -12V
label printed on the module and on your case’s PSU busboard.
If you cannot align both the key/notch and the redline/-12V label, find a new ribbon
cable. After double checking the ribbon cable, place the module in your case and secure
it with the screws of your choosing.
Who is Gilbert?
Gilbert is a wavefolder and modulation hub. Patch programming is the M.O.
Gilbert is DC coupled, capable of processing both CV and audio. It's functionality is
limited only by the creativity of the user. Some uses include wavefolding, frequency
multiplication, multi-channel crossfading, and multi-channel signal routing. On paper
Gilbert may seem esoteric, however in practice it is incredibly intuitive and easy to use.
There is one main input and four main outputs. As the input voltage increases from -5V
to +5V, four unipolar sinusoidal waveforms rise and fall sequentially at the four main
outputs. This allows a single CV source to generate four new control voltages that are
tailored for quadraphonic panning, multi-channel crossfading, and multi-channel signal
routing. Alternatively, these four new control voltages can sequentially modulate four
different parameters in your modular system, creating a lot of dynamic and complex
movement that all stems from a single CV source.

text.tspan: Defining the controls
The level parameter determines the amplitude of the
signal applied to Gilbert's main input, labeled "in".
When the level panel control is positioned fully counter
clockwise, the input signal is reduced to an amplitude
of 0V. When the level panel control is positioned fully
clockwise, the input signal is at unity gain.

text.tspan: Gilbert is calibrated such that a waveform with an amplitude of +/- 5V will activate all
four main outputs. So by positioning the bias control at noon and the level control fully
clockwise, a Eurorack standard LFO will cyclically activate all four main outputs.
The level panel control is accompanied by a neighboring CV input. CV applied to this
input modulates the level parameter and sums with the position of the level panel
control. The expected range of this sum is 10V.
The animation below illustrates sweeping the level panel control across its entire range
in low gain mode. The bias control is positioned at 12 o'clock (0V). Note how the
different outputs gradually activate as the input signal's amplitude increases.
Standards
All parameters on shkrjn-instruments modules are designed to respond to a range of 10V.
Think of it this way: a knob that is fully counter clockwise corresponds to 0V and a knob
that is fully clockwise corresponds to 10V. A knob positioned at 12 o’clock corresponds to
0V
5V
When a knob is marked with “O” directly above it, the 12 o’clock position corresponds to
0V. Thus the fully counter clockwise position corresponds to -5V, while the fully clockwise
position corresponds to 5V. The entire range of the knob is still 10V.
0V
5V
The same concept applies to attenuators. When an attenuator for a CV input is marked
with “O” directly above it, that indicates a bipolar attenuator, sometimes called an
attenuverter. This means that the 12 o’clock position corresponds to no modulation, while
the fully counter clockwise position corresponds to 100% inverted modulation and the
fully clockwise position corresponds to 100% non inverted modulation.
When an attenuator is not accompanied by “O”, that indicates a standard unipolar
attenuator. The fully counter clockwise position corresponds to no modulation, while the
fully clockwise position corresponds to 100% modulation.
Imagine that a parameter's panel control is positioned at 12 o’clock and the parameter is
being modulated by a bipolar LFO with a range of +/- 5V. This has the same effect as
sweeping that knob across its entire range from fully counter-clockwise to fully clockwise:
Imagine that the same panel control is positioned fully counter clockwise and the
associated parameter is modulated by a unipolar envelope with an amplitude of 10V. This
also has the same effect of sweeping that knob across its entire range from counter
clockwise to clockwise.
This is the behavior that is being described when you encounter the following text: “CV
applied to the X input sums with the X knob position after it passes through the bipolar
attenuator. The expected range of this sum is 10V.”
The Gain switch toggles between high gain mode and low gain mode. High gain mode
engages additional folding stages, which allows Gilbert to achieve richer and more
complex timbres when it is being used as a wavefolder. Gilbert MK2 can achieve three
times as much wavefolding as Gilbert MK1. Low gain mode is ideal for when Gilbert is
processing CV because it allows for finer control over which of the four main outputs are
activated. The gain switch has no effect on the bias control.
Position the gain switch upwards to activate high gain mode
Position the gain switch downwards to activate low gain mode
gain
gain
The bias parameter adjusts an internal DC offset that is
summed with the input signal, post VCA. The bias panel
control has a range of +/- 5V, with the 12 o'clock position
corresponding to 0V.
Bias has many uses. When Gilbert is processing audio,
bias acts as a "symmetry" control, creating interesting timbres through asymmetric
wavefolding. When Gilbert is processing CV, bias determines the initial output that is
activated by the input signal. Bias can also determine which outputs are activated by the
input signal, depending on input signal's amplitude.
The best way to understand how bias works is to reduce the the input level control to 0
and then sweep the bias panel control across its entire range, watching the four main
outputs activate sequentially. Then patch a triangle LFO to Gilbert's input and gradually
increase the level control while continuing to adjust bias. Take note of the output activity
for various positions of both level and bias.
CV applied to the bias input modulates the bias parameter. This CV sums directly with
the bias panel control. The expected range of this sum is +/-5V (10V).
The animation below illustrates a common use of the bias control. By reducing the
amplitude of the input signal, Gilbert will alternate between two outputs. The bias
control can then be used to determine which of the two outputs Gilbert is alternating
between.
out level

text.tspan: The out level parameter determines the amplitude of all of the outputs
via a global VCA. When the out level panel control is positioned fully
counter clockwise, all of the outputs are reduced to 0V. When the out
level panel control is positioned fully clockwise, the four main outputs
have a range of 0 - 10V, while the fold output has a range of +/- 5V.
The global VCA can be modulated via the panel control's accomapnying
CV input. CV applied to this input directly sums with the out level panel
control. The expected range of this sum is 10V.
Modulating the out level is a great way to add complexity to your patches. When Gilbert
is processing CV, modulating the out level will vary the modulation depth of the newly
generated CV. When Gilbert is processing audio, modulating the out level will adjust the
volume of the fold output. The out level can act as the final VCA for your synth voice by
positioning the out level panel control fully counter clockwise and applying an envelope
to the CV input.

text.tspan: The two images below illustrate the difference between high gain mode and low gain
mode when monitoring the fold output. The blue triangle wave is the signal applied to
Gilbert's input and the gold sine wave is Gilbert's fold output. Assume that the input
level control is positioned fully clockwise, the bias control is positioned at 12 o'clock,
and the output level control is positioned fully clockwise. The top image shows low gain
mode and bottom image shows high gain mode.
Gilbert MK2 features many improvements over Gilbert MK1:
High quality discrete input VCA, providing voltage control over the input level
Redesigned global output VCA, which improves offness and eliminates CV bleed
High gain mode to activate additional folding stages
Bidirectional circular activiation of the four main outputs
CV input for the bias control
Factory assembled with surface mount components
Reverse power protection

text.tspan: Patch a triangle LFO to the main input. Assuming that the LFO has a
range of +/- 5V, position the level panel control fully clockwise and the
bias control at 12 o'clock. As the LFO cycles, watch the LEDs fade in
and out. The LED's varying brightness indicates the rising and falling
voltage at each output. If the LEDs are not lit, ensure that the output
level panel control is positioned fully clockwise.
Patch the four main outputs so that they are modulating four different
parameters in your modular system. Listen to these parameters vary as
the initial LFO cycles. Vary the depth of this modulation by adjusting
the output level via the panel control or the CV input.
By attenuating the input signal, you can limit how many of Gilbert's
outputs are active. Turn the level panel control counter clockwise until
only two LEDs are alternating back and forth. Adjust the bias control to
determine which two LEDs are alternating while listening to the
modulation associated with the alternating outputs. Apply a second
LFO, that is slower than the initial LFO, to the bias CV input and listen
to modulation increase in complexity.
By using the four main outputs to modulate four different VCAs, the user is able to
continuously crossfade between four different audio sources. By adjusting the input
level control and the bias control, the user is able to limit the amount of channels they
are crossfading between and between which channels they are crossfading.
Find an audio rate triangle wave and apply it to Gilbert’s input. Assuming this
waveform has a range of +/- 5V, position the bias control at noon, while also
positioning the input level control fully clockwise and the gain switch down. Apply
Gilbert’s fold output to the final output of your modular system, while ensuring the
output level control is positioned fully clockwise.
While listening to the output, gradually turn the input level control counterclockwise.
You should hear the timbre of the output waveform gradually become less complex
and then fade into silence.
Push the gain switch up and repeat the process, listening to the increased amount of
wavefolding. Next, adjust the input level control so that only two LEDs are lit. Sweep
the bias control across its entire range while listening to how this affects the timbre of
the output.
While using Gilbert as an audio processor, the input level control is the same as the
“timbre” or “fold” controls that are found on dedicated wave folders, while the bias
control is the same as a “symmetry”, or “offset” controls.
Gilbert MKii features a discrete input VCA and a CV input for the bias control. Gilbert
MKi required several additional modules to achieve the aforementioned “fold” and
“symmetry” modulation. Now there is no need for external modules. Simply patch CV
to the input level’s CV input to modulate “fold” and patch CV to the bias CV input to
modulate “symmetry”.
Gilbert’s output level control can act as the final VCA for this patch by positioning the
panel control fully counterclockwise and then applying an envelope to the associated
CV input.
The animation below demonstrates monitoring the fold output while sweeping the
input level control across its entire range in high gain mode.
The four main outputs are internally processed through a bipolar mixer, the output of
which is provided at the fold output. This creates a new bipolar waveform that allows
Gilbert to function as a voltage controlled wavefolder or frequency multiplier. By
increasing the input level, the input waveform is gradually transformed into a sine wave,
which is then continuously folded over, creating new harmonics and increasing in timbral
complexity. Gilbert MK2 offers a high gain mode, which activates additional folding
stages, providing three times as much wavefolding as the Mk1 version.
